rationale.conceptual: The method combines established fracture mechanics principles (quarter-point crack-tip elements, triaxiality parameter h) with a specific mesh design (50 through-thickness layers, 1 µm surface layer, geometric progression). Implementing this correctly requires careful understanding of FE discretisation and stress extraction, going beyond a simple textbook example, but it is not a novel research algorithm.
rationale.execution: The pipeline involves several stages: parametric mesh generation, solver execution for 10–15 geometry combinations, extraction of nodal stresses, computation of h and pt, and aggregation into a CSV. Coordinating these steps and handling solver I/O adds engineering complexity, but the tools are standard and the sweep is modest.

difficulty.reasoning: The task requires implementing a standard 3D linear elastic finite element analysis of a notched M(T) specimen using a specific mesh refinement scheme, running a parametric sweep across geometry, and computing stress triaxiality. No novel algorithms are invented, but the mesh generation details (quarter-point singular elements, spider-web, through-thickness grading) and the multi-step orchestration (mesh → solver → postprocess → CSV) make it a moderately complex but well-documented engineering mechanics reproduction.

compute_estimate.reasoning: A single simulation uses a direct solver on a mesh with ~116k nodes; peak RAM is a few GB. All data are generated parametrically; no external large datasets are involved. Runs are wholly CPU-based.
